prompt: In an unweighted graph, why does breadth-first search (BFS) always find a shortest path between two nodes, while depth-first search (DFS) is not guaranteed to?
choices: BFS runs in O(1) time while DFS runs in O(V+E) time, so BFS finishes before it can find a longer path

BFS explores nodes in increasing order of distance from the source, layer by layer, so the first time it reaches the target is guaranteed to be via a shortest path; DFS commits to one branch and follows it all the way down before backtracking, so it can reach the target via a much longer route first
DFS is only allowed to visit each node once, while BFS can revisit nodes to find a shorter route
BFS uses a stack internally and DFS uses a queue, and stack-based traversal is inherently shorter

prompt:
Your cache's get method looks like this:

def get(self, key):
    if key not in self.table:
        return None
    node = self.table[key]
    self._move_to_front(node)  # O(1) pointer surgery on a doubly linked list
    return node.value

self.table is your own hash table with O(1) average-case lookup, and _move_to_front does O(1) pointer surgery on a doubly linked list. What is the average-case time complexity of this get call?
You build an LRU cache with capacity 2 and run this sequence: put(1, "a"); put(2, "b"); get(1); put(3, "c"); get(2). What does that final get(2) call return?
This module's cache project requires building get/put on top of your own hash table instead of using Python's dict, collections.OrderedDict, or functools.lru_cache. Why?
choices: Because Python's dict does not provide O(1) average-case lookups

Because the exercise is specifically about combining a hash table with a recency-tracking structure yourself to get O(1) average-case eviction — reaching for a built-in cache skips exactly the design work being practiced
Because collections.OrderedDict was removed in recent versions of Python
Because functools.lru_cache cannot be given a custom capacity
